title: Polynomial multiplication over Z_p: schoolbook vs number-theoretic transform (FFT)
problem_statement: Given two polynomials A and B with n coefficients each in Z_p (p = 998244353), compute the 2n - 1 coefficients of A * B mod p.

input.parameter: n = number of coefficients of each polynomial.
input.size_measure: 2n elements of Z_p (30-bit words; arithmetic is unit cost).

algorithms.name: schoolbook convolution
algorithms.idea: C[i + j] += A[i] * B[j] for all pairs (i, j).
algorithms.pseudocode: for i, j: C[i+j] = (C[i+j] + A[i] B[j]) mod p
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) in the worst case: exactly z n coefficient multiplications and Theta(n (1 + z)) time for z non-zero coefficients of A, so exactly n^2 multiplications when no coefficient of A is 0 (and Theta(n) when A = 0)

algorithms.name: number-theoretic transform (Cooley-Tukey over Z_p)
algorithms.idea: Evaluate A and B at the 2^k-th roots of unity in Z_p with a radix-2 FFT, multiply pointwise, and interpolate with the inverse transform.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n). Exact count used for V2: 3 n log2(n) + 5 n multiplications on input-derived values for n a power of two with n >= 2 (n = 1 gives 2; see verification.method)
algorithms.correctness: The DFT over Z_p diagonalises cyclic convolution (the DFT of a cyclic convolution is the pointwise product of the DFTs, since w^N = 1). p is prime, p - 1 = 119 * 2^23 and 3 is a primitive root, so primitive 2^k-th roots of unity exist for k <= 23 (sizes up to 2^23), and padding to size >= 2n - 1 makes cyclic convolution equal to the ordinary product; correct for n <= 2^22, where the transform size is at most 2^23 (PROOFS.md sections 5-7, which also prove that the bit-reversed iterative transform computes the DFT and that the inverse transform inverts it; Cooley & Tukey 1965 for the FFT recursion).

relationship: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n). The use of fast transforms over rings in integer multiplication is background (see background).

background.statement: Schoenhage and Strassen base integer multiplication on a fast Fourier transform.

sources.authors: Cooley, J. W.; Tukey, J. W.
sources.title: An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series

sources.authors: Heideman, M. T.; Johnson, D. H.; Burrus, C. S.
sources.title: Gauss and the history of the fast Fourier transform
sources.note: History of the fast Fourier transform (per its title).

verification.method: V1: both agree on random polynomials, n = 0..257 (including sizes just above powers of two, which force padding), and pass an independent check A(x) B(x) = C(x) mod p at three fixed points. V2 by exact multiplication counts (measure 'reported', round 2026-10-06c). generate_scaling draws the same coefficients as generate() and wraps each in an int-like type that propagates through +, -, * and % and counts every multiplication with at least one input-derived operand; the implementations are unchanged and return the same coefficients on the counting type (experiments/2026-10-06c_ntt_counts.py). Schoolbook: exactly n^2 on every measured n (no zero coefficient was drawn); alpha = 1.000 against n^2 at tolerance 0.03, rivals n log n (1.697) and n^2 log n (0.918) rejected. NTT (n a power of two, so padding is exactly 2n): exactly 3 n log2(n) + 5 n for n = 2^3..2^15, namely (log2(2n) - 1) n per forward transform (in the first stage every butterfly has a padding zero, a plain int), 2n pointwise products, and log2(2n) n butterfly products plus 2n scalings in the inverse transform. The cost expression is this exact form (RL-062); alpha = 1.000 at tolerance 0.03, rivals n (1.111), n log^2 n (0.885) and n^2 (0.555) rejected, so the log factor is resolved. The leading term n log n alone gives alpha = 0.985 on the same counts. The earlier timing fit could not separate n log n from n (RL-018). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry from the code (the correctness of both algorithms, with the primality of p, the roots of unity, the bit-reversed iterative transform and its inverse; the domain n <= 2^22; the time and space bounds; the exact counts for all sizes of their domains) and names the scripts and tests that check each one, among them tests/test_proofs_ntt.py.

caveats: The V2 count sees only multiplications with an input-derived operand. Not counted: the NTT's twiddle-factor updates w * w_len (one per butterfly) and pow() calls, which work on plain ints the implementation creates from literals; the first-stage butterfly products whose operand is a padding zero; and all additions, subtractions and reductions mod p in both algorithms. In the NTT every counted butterfly product has a plain-int twiddle factor; only the pointwise products (2n of them for n a power of two, n >= 2) have two input-derived operands.
